name: Galileo Probe
intro: The Galileo Probe was the first spacecraft to dive into a giant planet’s air. On 7 December 1995 it plunged into Jupiter, radioed data for about 58 minutes, then was crushed and melted. Nothing is left, so this model is a memorial above Jupiter’s clouds.
whyLeft: It was always a one-way dive: Jupiter has no ground to land on. It sank until the heat and pressure silenced it, as planned.
repurpose: Nothing is left to repair. Its job was to measure Jupiter’s air on the way down, and it did, until the very end.

hotspots.title: The heat shield
hotspots.text: The probe hit Jupiter’s air at about 170,000 km/h, the fastest entry ever. Its thick heat shield glowed hotter than the surface of the Sun, and much of it burned away, as planned.

photo.alt: A round metal descent module hanging above a ring-shaped shell in a workshop.
photo.caption: The Galileo Probe being put together on Earth: the descent module, which carried the instruments, above the shell that shielded it.
photo.licenseEvidence: Commons page licence: “Public domain” (PD NASA); original source: https://ails.arc.nasa.gov/ (image link).

hotspots.title: The parachute
hotspots.text: Once it had slowed down, the probe threw off its back cover and opened a parachute, then dropped its heat shield and drifted down through the clouds.

hotspots.title: Tasting Jupiter’s air
hotspots.text: Instruments inside sniffed the gases and measured the winds. They found far less water than expected, and winds deep down even stronger than at the cloud tops.

hotspots.title: The last signal
hotspots.text: The probe radioed its findings up to Galileo for about 58 minutes. Then the heat and crushing pressure, about 23 times Earth’s air pressure, silenced it.

funFact: Slowing down from 170,000 km/h, the probe felt a squeeze up to 228 times its own weight on Earth.
